#113935. FDIC Insurance Covers $250,000 per Ownership Category – Not Everything Your Bank Sells

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (490 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

FDIC Insurance Covers $250,000 per Ownership Category – Not Everything Your Bank Sells

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts.
  • A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover.
  • According to recent reports, deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts. It doesn’t cover stocks, mutual funds, annuities, or crypto, even when you buy them at the bank. Confirm your bank on the FDIC’s BankFind, then total each category in its EDIE estimator.

A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover. The branch that opens your savings account may also sell you an annuity, and a CD you open later can push your total past the limit.

According to recent reports, deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for. But the FDIC doesn’t cover bonds, life insurance, or the contents of a safe deposit box. A money market deposit account counts as a deposit, while a money market fund, despite the similar name, is an investment with no FDIC coverage.

An ownership category is the way you own an account. The common ones are single accounts in your name alone, joint accounts, retirement accounts such as IRAs, and trust accounts, which include a savings account or CD naming a beneficiary to inherit it. Each category is insured on its own, but all your accounts in one category at one bank share one limit, whether they’re checking, savings, or CDs. Opening one at another branch of the same bank doesn’t change that.

It has been revealed that take a saver with two accounts at one bank, both in her name alone with no beneficiary. Her savings account holds $180,000, and her CD holds $90,000. Both are single accounts, so the FDIC adds them together, and her $270,000 is $20,000 over the limit. She could name a beneficiary on the CD, which would make it a trust account with its own limit, or move $20,000 to a different insured bank.

To check your own coverage, search the FDIC’s BankFind by your bank’s name or web address to confirm it’s insured. Then enter each account’s balance and owners in EDIE, the FDIC’s Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator, which shows what’s insured at that bank and any amount over the limit. For a money app that isn’t a bank, look up the bank behind it instead.

Leave room under each category’s limit for at least a year of interest, since interest counts toward the limit through the day a bank fails.

Recent findings suggest that having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

If you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That mentioned, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

Industry observers note that no matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data shows the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

To save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

Industry observers note that the next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment prepares.

If you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment prepares and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

Sources indicate that once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

According to recent reports, then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

In a recent development, it’s important to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as quickly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

In a recent development, finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

Industry observers note that how much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Recent findings suggest that having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

According to recent reports, in the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

Pay for a new business with savings and side income before you borrow or take on investors, and leave your emergency fund and retirement accounts out of it. Your own money costs no interest and gives no one a share of what you build. Keep your job until sales show the business can pay you.

A new business often loses money for months before it turns a profit. Paying for that stretch yourself means a slow start costs you time, not a loan payment you can’t make.

Your job makes that possible. Its paycheck covers your household, so the business doesn’t have to pay you yet and can reinvest every dollar it earns. Earn your side income in the field you plan to enter. Each sale then adds to the startup fund and indicates whether strangers will pay for what you sell, before you sign a lease.

Picture a baker who keeps her office job and sells at weekend markets for a year. Saving $1,000 a month from her paycheck and making about $1,100 a month in market profits, she has roughly $25,000 by year’s end, enough to open a small storefront with used ovens without owing anyone. A year of sales has also shown her which breads customers buy.

According to recent reports, to size the fund, add up the business’s opening costs plus several months of running costs. The Small Business Administration’s guide to startup costs lists the usual ones, from permits to insurance, and offers a fillable worksheet. If the total is out of reach, start smaller, with a market stall before a storefront or used equipment before new.

Leave your emergency fund alone, because it keeps the household afloat if the business stalls or your job ends. Retirement accounts are expensive to tap early. A withdrawal from a 401(k) or traditional IRA before age 59½ usually costs income tax plus a 10% penalty. Even Roth IRA contributions, which come out anytime without tax or penalty, stop growing for retirement once withdrawn.

Grow the fund faster by saving a bigger share of each paycheck and selling what you no longer use, and keep it in its own high-yield savings account, apart from your emergency fund.

Open that account this week and schedule a transfer into it for every payday, so the money is saved before you can spend it.

Discount sites, shoe chains’ online clearance sections, and brands’ own sale pages sell brand-name shoes for less, but the return terms decide whether a bad fit costs you. Before you order a size you haven’t worn, check the return window and the cost of a mailed return, since several sellers charge $8.50 to $9.99.

Shoes in the same size fit differently from one brand to the next, and even between models from one brand, so a pair ordered online is a guess until the box arrives.

Return terms split the eight sellers below into three groups. Three pay for a mailed return, though one does so only for members and another only in the lower 48 states. Three more take returns free in their stores but deduct $8.50 or $9.95 from a refund by mail, and the last two make you pay for every return you mail.

Here are the eight, from the friendliest return terms to the costliest:.

The sellers with free mail returns make it cheap to order two sizes and keep one. Say you’re between a 10 and a 10.5 in a $140 running shoe from Running Warehouse. Order both, try them on a clean floor, keep the pair that fits, and send the other back with the prepaid label from the box. You pay $280 up front, $140 comes back once the refund posts, and the return costs nothing. From a seller that deducts $9.95 by mail, the same order at the same price leaves the pair you keep costing $149.95.

In a recent development, keep any try-on indoors, since most of these sellers refund only unworn pairs. Zappos also wants its shoe box back without tape or postal labels, so pack it inside a shipping box.

Buy a size you’re unsure of from Zappos, Running Warehouse, or Nike as a member, or from DSW, Famous Footwear, or Nordstrom Rack when one of their stores is near you. Save 6pm and Joe’s New Balance Outlet for a model you already own in the right size.

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • Industry observers note that “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun upcoming way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which mentioned something like,.

Industry observers note that “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

Sources indicate that so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

Industry observers note that but occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

In a recent development, I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

In a recent development, then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

Industry observers note that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

In a recent development, experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning upcoming things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

Industry observers note that one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

It has been revealed that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if a bank turned your business down, apply for an SBA microloan of up to $50,000 from a nonprofit lender on the SBA’s list of microlenders. These lenders also coach borrowers on marketing and management. The money can buy equipment, inventory, or supplies, but it can’t pay off debt or buy real estate.

The SBA funds these lenders but doesn’t review your credit. Each lender decides who qualifies and sets your rate and terms.

In a recent development, A microloan tops out at $50,000, carries a fixed rate, and must be repaid within seven years. The SBA states rates usually run 8% to 13%. The business can be brand fresh, but it must be a for-profit small business in the U.S. Since April 2026, an SBA policy also requires every owner to be a U.S. citizen or national whose main home is in the U.S., which rules out green card holders.

In a recent development, SBA rules let a lender go past $20,000 only after you show that the business can’t get credit elsewhere at a comparable rate and that it’s likely to succeed. A bank’s rejection in writing helps you show the first.

The money can also serve as working capital, the cash that runs the business day to day, or pay for furniture, fixtures, and machinery.

Sources indicate that say a mobile dog groomer turned down by her bank borrows $18,000 at a fixed 9% over five years to outfit a van. Her payment would be about $374 a month, and she’d pay about $4,420 in interest over the loan.

Industry observers note that the coaching can start before you borrow. Lenders can spend up to half of their SBA coaching grants on people who haven’t borrowed yet.

Find lenders on the SBA’s list of microlenders, filtered to your state, and call two or three for help with your application. Ask each for its rate, what property it would hold as collateral, and whether you’d sign a personal guarantee, which makes you personally responsible for the loan.

For a loan outside the microloan program, compare the best small business loans and SBA lenders or the nonprofit lender Accion Opportunity Fund.

Card issuers normally can’t raise the rate on a balance you already owe, but a rise in that index is one of the exceptions, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes. On a $10,000 card balance carried all year, each percentage point added to the rate costs about $100 in interest.

Sources indicate that online banks have passed more of each increase on to savers. Pay down card balances first, then a HELOC ahead of any fixed-rate loan charging the same rate or less. If you’ll borrow for a car or a home soon, lock in a fixed rate before you buy.

Sources indicate that keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account. For fresh certificates of deposit (CDs), stick to terms of a year or less until rates level off, or build a CD ladder so part of your money comes due every six months.

SBA Loans Cost Less Than Online Business Loans – If You Can Wait Weeks

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks.
  • Sources indicate that owners turn to online lenders for speed.
  • Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks. The SBA’s guarantee comes with a capped rate and terms up to 10 years for most uses, 25 for real estate. Expect to pledge collateral on loans over $50,000, sign a personal guarantee, and, as a startup, put in at least 10% of the cost.

Sources indicate that owners turn to online lenders for speed. In the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Small Business Credit Survey, 60% of firms that borrowed from online lenders said their borrowing costs ran higher than expected, against 32% of large-bank borrowers.

An SBA loan is slower and cheaper. The U.S. Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make. In return for that backing, SBA rules cap a variable rate at the banks’ benchmark prime rate, now 7.00%, plus 3 to 6.5 percentage points, depending on the loan’s size.

Say a landscaper owes $120,000 on online term loans repaid over two years at 30% interest, about $6,710 a month. A 10-year 7(a) loan at a fixed 11% cuts that to about $1,650. The longer term costs more interest in total, about $78,000 over 10 years against $41,000 on the online loans. Extra payments shrink that, and a 7(a) loan shorter than 15 years carries no prepayment fee.

It has been revealed that A 7(a) loan of up to $5 million can cover working capital, equipment, real estate, debt refinancing, or starting or buying a business. A 504 loan, made through a nonprofit Certified Development Company, finances buildings, land, and long-lived machinery at a fixed rate. SBA microloans of up to $50,000 come from nonprofit lenders.

Under the SBA’s lending rules, every owner of 20% or more personally guarantees the whole loan, and a loan over $50,000 needs collateral, though a lender can’t refuse you for weak collateral alone. A business open a year or less must put in at least 10% of the total cost, and so must most buyers of a business.

In a recent development, to get an SBA loan, start with a bank that knows your business, and ask whether it’s an SBA Preferred Lender, one allowed to approve loans without the SBA’s review, which can take up to 10 business days. Or describe your needs in the SBA’s Lender Match tool, which lists interested lenders two business days later.

Apply once you know a substantial cost is coming, and keep online loans for needs that can’t wait weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that buy your next rental where rent is high against home prices. In 15 Midwest and Southern metros, a typical house rents for 7.4% to 11.2% of its value a year. Before you offer, check the city’s taxes, insurance, and vacancy, and what houses on that street actually rent for.

Sources indicate that that share, a year’s rent divided by the price, is the gross yield, and it decides whether rent can cover a mortgage. In Zillow’s October 2026 figures, a typical house in the San Diego area rents for about 5% of its value a year, while one in the McAllen, Texas, area rents for 11.2%.

According to recent reports, now figure the mortgage payment on each, with 25% down and a 30-year loan at 7%. A typical McAllen-area house, worth $189,000, rents for about $1,760 a month, roughly $820 more than its $943 payment. A typical San Diego-area house, worth about $1 million, rents for about $4,130, about $860 short of its payment of nearly $5,000.

According to recent reports, at those terms, the typical rent is higher than the mortgage payment in all 15 metros below, by about $270 a month in Little Rock up to about $820 in McAllen. That margin still has to pay the property taxes and insurance, plus the repairs, empty months, and management every landlord budgets for, so those costs decide whether a house makes money.

Since October 2023, typical rents have risen faster than typical home prices, so the yield on a typical U.S. house has climbed from 7.0% to 7.4%.

Each price, rent, and yield here covers a whole metro area and uses Zillow’s typical single-family home value and rent, the middle of each market. Every metro on the list passed six tests:.

Two significant Texas metros fell short. San Antonio’s typical rent rose only 0.7% over the past year, and Census’s metro estimates put Dallas’s rental vacancy at 14.7% this summer, nearly twice the national rate.

Here they are, from the highest yield down, with each metro’s typical house value and monthly rent.

According to recent reports, property taxes come out of the rent every year, and several states on this list tax a rental more heavily than an owner’s home. Texas’s homestead exemptions, which shield part of a home’s value from tax, go only to an owner’s main home, so a rental in McAllen or El Paso is taxed on its full value, the state comptroller explains. Michigan charges a rental up to 18 mills, or $18 per $1,000 of taxable value, in school operating taxes that an owner’s home skips, according to its Treasury Department.

Recent findings suggest that in South Carolina, a rental is assessed at 6% of its value, against 4% for an owner’s home, and pays school operating taxes the owner’s home skips, as Richland County, home to Columbia, explains. Indiana caps a rental’s yearly property tax at 2% of its assessed value, against 1% for an owner’s home, according to the state’s Department of Local Government Finance.

Sources indicate that insurance is the other significant cost that varies by state. In Insurance.com’s 2026 study of quoted rates for a standard policy with $300,000 of coverage on the house, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Kansas averaged more than $5,000 a year, about twice the $2,872 national average. Texas averaged $4,582. Get a quote on a landlord policy for the exact house before you offer.

Landlord law matters as well. Oregon, Washington, and California cap yearly rent increases statewide, while 36 states bar their cities from adopting rent control at all, according to the National Apartment Association, a landlords’ trade group.

Every number above describes a whole metro, which mixes blocks where houses rent rapidly with blocks where they sit empty. Before you offer, compare the rent the seller quotes with what similar houses nearby actually rent for. If you’re buying in another state, have a local agent or property manager pull those rents for you.

Start with the two or three metros whose typical prices fit your budget, and run one real listing in each through the mortgage test above, using its own tax bill and insurance quote.

A grant is the cheapest money a business can get, since you never repay it and no one takes a share of the firm.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Small Business Administration “does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business,” according to its own grants page. The federal grants a tech giant can win go mostly to research, through the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs, and to exporters.

So for a shop, a restaurant, or a service business, the grants worth chasing are local.

Recent findings suggest that take a bakery owner who searches the federal grant listings and finds research and export programs, nothing for a bakery. Her city’s economic development office runs a storefront program that pays back half the cost of exterior work, up to $10,000. She applies before hiring anyone, as the program requires, wins a grant, spends $16,000 on a upcoming sign, awning, and lighting, and gets $8,000 back once the work is done.

Here’s where to look, starting close to home, with what each source pays for and who can apply.

According to recent reports, A real government grant never charges you a fee. The Federal Trade Commission says no agency will reach out to demand that you pay for a grant, and it warns against paying any up-front fee.

It also warns against paying for a list of grants, since the complete list of federal grants on Grants.gov is free.

Check the sender, too. The SBA states it writes only from email addresses ending in @sba.gov, and that anyone claiming to be the agency from another address should be reported as fraud.

Read what the grant pays for first, since many fund a single purpose. Philadelphia’s Storefront Improvement Program covers exterior work such as signs, awnings, lighting, and paint, and STEP money goes only to export activities the SBA approves.

Recent findings suggest that then check what you’d have to put in yourself. Philadelphia’s program pays back up to half the cost of approved work, so you cover at least half and pay the whole bill until the city reimburses you. USDA’s Value-Added Producer Grants require a dollar-for-dollar match.

Many grants also want a business that’s already running. STEP is for established small businesses, and the $25,000 Wells Fargo grants the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce offered in 2026 required two years in business.

The competition is steep. Boston’s storefront program says it lacks the money to give a grant to every eligible business, and Hiring Our Heroes names five winners a round. Winning takes an application that answers the funder’s scoring criteria point by point.

Start with one call to your city’s economic development office, and ask which grants it’s funding this year, what each one pays for, and how much of the cost you’d have to cover.

It has been revealed that you land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

According to recent reports, do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

It has been revealed that avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Industry observers note that avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. According to recent reports, do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. According to recent reports, families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. Sources indicate that this redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Sources indicate that midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Recent findings suggest that virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Sources indicate that yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • In a recent development, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

In a recent development, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

Recent findings suggest that but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

In a recent development, yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

Recent findings suggest that so I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s latest manufacturer, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

Industry observers note that and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

In a recent development, this is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

Sources indicate that in many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

It has been revealed that but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

According to recent reports, distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

Industry observers note that and while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

Industry observers note that so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty swiftly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Recent findings suggest that many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term aims again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

Sources indicate that when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that states, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the concern, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

Recent findings suggest that the modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

Sources indicate that more modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

Recent findings suggest that and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The manufacturer that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

According to recent reports, in the Comments: Do you have questions about hormone replacement or anything else in this article? I’ll try to invite Kevin, Dr. Sean Bender and other knowledgeable people to contribute and answer questions as well.

  • In a recent development, the comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF).
  • Industry observers note that the catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that teach full time for five school years in a row at a low-income school, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness can cancel up to $17,500 of your subsidized and unsubsidized federal loans, depending on your subject. But those years can’t also count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which has no cap, so compare the two before you apply.

In a recent development, the comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF). Secondary math and science teachers and elementary or secondary special education teachers can get up to $17,500, and other teachers up to $5,000.

Industry observers note that the catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF). PSLF cancels whatever federal Direct Loan balance remains after 120 qualifying monthly payments, made over at least 10 years at a public school or another qualifying employer. Take TLF, and your payments from those five years stop counting toward PSLF, so you’d need 120 more.

For a small balance, TLF beats waiting for PSLF. A high school math teacher who borrowed $16,000 can have what’s left canceled after year five, since it’s under her cap. A colleague who also teaches math aims to stay in public schools and repay on an income-driven proposal, which sets payments by income. With $60,000 in loans, she’d get at most $17,500 from TLF and likely far more from PSLF at year 10, so she skips TLF.

Before you count on TLF, confirm three things:.

With a balance under your cap, you can ask your loan servicer each year for a TLF forbearance, which pauses payments so you don’t pay down debt TLF would cancel. Interest still builds and can push your balance past the cap.

After year five, have your principal, superintendent, or HR office certify the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Application, then send it to your servicer, one form per servicer.

Before you choose, use StudentAid.gov’s Repayment Calculator to compare what you’d pay in total under each program, since TLF can’t be undone after it’s granted.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes.
  • A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference highlights up the first time a payment is late.
  • Start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes. Set the rate at or above the applicable federal rate, a minimum the IRS publishes monthly, so no part of the loan counts as a gift.

A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference highlights up the first time a payment is late.

Start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule. Money your parents don’t want back is a gift, and a parent who gives you more than the annual gift tax exclusion in one year files a gift tax return. If they want a share of the profits, it’s a stake, which makes them part owners who get nothing back if the business fails.

If the loan charges less than the applicable federal rate (AFR), the IRS’s below-market loan rules can treat the interest your parents gave up as a gift from them. In some cases, the IRS also counts it as income they owe tax on.

It has been revealed that in the note, formally a promissory note, two terms need the most thought. The first is whether you or your business owes it. Money lent to your limited liability tech giant (LLC) is generally its debt, not yours, so your parents carry the risk if it closes. The second is what happens to the balance if the business closes, whether you keep paying from your own income, pause the payments, or your parents forgive the rest.

Sources indicate that say a son borrows $20,000 from his parents for four years. The IRS’s mid-term rate applies to loans over three years and up to nine. Suppose that rate is just under 5% when he gets the money, so they charge 5%. Forty-eight automatic transfers of about $461 repay it with about $2,100 in interest, and no one has to bring up a payment at a holiday dinner.

Recent findings suggest that ask for no more than your parents could afford to give away, since a new business can close before it repays anyone. Then give them a few days to decide how to lend without losing money or the relationship.

Look up the AFR for the month you get the money, write a rate at least that high into the note, and set up the automatic transfer the day it arrives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pay for startup equipment and inventory with a business credit card that charges 0% interest on purchases for a year or more. Divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that payment on autopay, so your card is paid off before its regular rate starts.

Industry observers note that borrowing at 0% costs less than most startup loans. A microloan through the U.S. Small Business Administration, for one, generally charges 8% to 13% interest, depending on the lender.

It has been revealed that the catch is that the debt is yours. Small-business cards typically carry a personal guarantee, so you and the business both owe the balance, a Federal Reserve report to Congress found. When the business has little or no credit history, the issuer relies more on your personal credit.

Sources indicate that the same report explains that the protections in the CARD Act, the 2009 federal law on credit card practices, apply to personal cards, not business cards. So your card’s own terms decide what a late payment costs. On U.S. Bank’s Business Shield, one late payment, or one that bounces, ends the 0% rate early.

Charge only purchases that will bring in money soon, like the equipment you’ll work with and inventory you’ll sell. Months of rent and other bills are a poor fit, since a slow launch may not earn enough to repay them before the 0% rate ends.

The longer the 0% period, the smaller each monthly payment can be. Bank of America’s Platinum Plus business card gives 0% for 15 billing cycles on purchases when you apply online, then a variable rate of 14.99% to 25.99%. The 0% period starts when the account opens, so apply when you’re ready to buy.

Sources indicate that then divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that amount on autopay, the same plan that pays off a balance transfer in time. A photographer who charges $8,400 in cameras and lenses to a card with 0% for 15 months would pay $560 a month by that math. Rounding up to $600 clears it in 14 months, with a month to spare.

Set up that autopay the day the card arrives, so no payment comes in late while you’re busy launching.

From the best small-business credit cards, pick one whose 0% period is long enough for a payment your business can afford.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

According to recent reports, fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Recent findings suggest that make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important concerns for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

Sources indicate that in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

According to recent reports, your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That stated, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

In a recent development, while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Industry observers note that many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

Sources indicate that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

Startup Accelerators Cost You a Stake – Apply Only if You’ll Raise From Investors

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors.
  • According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant.
  • In a recent development, Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors. In exchange for a slice of your company, it usually gives you seed money, mentors, and introductions to investors. If you’ll never sell a stake, get free advice from SCORE or a Small Business Development Center instead.

According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant. Every dollar of it buys a piece of your organization.

In a recent development, Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts. Of that, $125,000 buys a fixed 7% of your tech giant, and Y Combinator invests the other $375,000 through a SAFE, a contract that turns into shares when investors later buy your stock at a set price. Techstars takes a fixed 5% for $20,000 and, in most programs, puts another $200,000 into the same kind of SAFE. Either way, the program’s stake grows past its fixed 7% or 5% once its SAFE turns into shares.

Along with the cash, that stake gets you mentors and introductions to investors. Many programs end with a demo day, where you pitch your organization to investors. That trade is worth making only if you’ll go on to raise money from angel investors or venture capital firms. A two-founder software startup that gives up a fixed 7%, then raises its first round from investors it met at demo day, gets what it paid for.

According to recent reports, A business that won’t raise from investors should look for help that costs no stake. Universities, cities, and companies run incubators that can offer workspace and advice. Some are free, while others charge a fee or take a stake, so ask first. A bakery that rents low-cost kitchen space from a city incubator and gets coaching there keeps the whole business. SCORE’s mentors advise U.S. business owners for free, and Small Business Development Centers offer no-cost consulting.

For a startup that will raise money, judge a program by its people and its terms. Find out which investors come to its demo day and whether its mentors have built companies like yours. Read the terms of both the fixed stake and the SAFE, and check whether you must move, since Y Combinator’s three-month program meets in person in San Francisco.

Before you apply, ask each program what share of the companies in its last two classes raised money within a year of demo day.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

A kid can watch a parent pay with a tap of a card all week and never see a bill, a loan balance, or an investment account.

A board game puts all three in front of them. In PayDay, a month of bills comes due on payday, and in Monopoly, a mortgaged property stops collecting rent. The game demonstrates a player what a choice cost. A question afterward about why they made it gets them to plan differently in the next game.

Each entry gives the ages its publisher recommends and what the game has players do with money.

It has been revealed that start with the ages on the box, then match the game’s length to how long your player will sit still. A game of Monopoly Deal can be over in 15 minutes, and Acquire runs about 90 minutes. PayDay’s rules let players choose how many months to play and say a three-month game with four players takes about an hour. Rich Dad says first-timers might need three to four hours for CASHFLOW.

For a shorter game of Monopoly, the rules in the box say to skip house rules: auction any property the player who lands on it won’t buy, never lend money between players, and put no cash on Free Parking.

Industry observers note that for a preschooler, a pretend store with real coins is the place to start. A younger sibling can join an older one’s game as a teammate who handles the money.

In a recent development, keep the talk short, and have it right after the game. Ask about one move that cost or made money, and let the player explain it before you add anything.

It has been revealed that picture a 10-year-old who comes up short at the end of a PayDay month. She borrows, then pays 10% of the loan every month after that. If she decides to set aside part of each month’s salary in the next game, she has worked out why a budget aims for bills before they arrive.

Tie the game to your family’s money too. A Monopoly rent payment is the moment to say what your household pays in rent or on its mortgage each month. A PayDay loan is the moment to show the interest rate on a credit card statement.

Set up a rematch within a week or two, so the player can try the change they described.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start with angel investors from your own industry, who bring advice and contacts along with the money. Reach them through local angel groups and introductions from founders they’ve backed. Before you take a check, work out what share of your firm the deal sells.

In a recent development, angels turn most founders down. They funded 22.6% of the deals brought to them in 2024, the University of Latest Hampshire’s Center for Venture Research found.

Most angel groups invest in markets where some of their members have expertise, the Angel Capital Association states. An angel who has worked in your field can judge your proposal swiftly and introduce you to customers and later investors.

In a recent development, search the association’s member directory, which lists angel groups by state and area of focus, and apply to the ones in your industry the way each group’s website asks. Ask founders in your field to introduce you to the angels who backed them, including any who lead a syndicate, which pools backers’ money into one check.

In a recent development, bring a short pitch and a one-page summary that show a large market and early traction, such as paying customers, and know your numbers cold. Take money only from accredited investors, who meet the SEC’s income, net-worth, or professional tests, since raising from anyone else brings extra disclosure rules.

Expect a SAFE, short for simple agreement for future equity, or less often a convertible note, a loan. Either usually turns into shares at your first priced round, the first time you sell shares at a set price. SAFEs made up 93% of the earliest-stage rounds on Carta, which tracks startup ownership, in the second quarter of 2026. On the standard SAFE, the angels’ share is at least their investment divided by the valuation cap, the highest company value the SAFE converts at. Six angels who put $250,000 into standard SAFEs with an $8 million cap would own at least 3.1% ($250,000 divided by $8 million) just before your priced round issues upcoming shares.

Sources indicate that most SAFEs convert right at their cap. Only 29% of priced seed rounds raised in 2026’s first nine months by startups with SAFEs converted those SAFEs below the cap, Carta’s latest report shows. Keep a running total of the share every SAFE takes, and have a startup lawyer read each one before you sign.
